name: Sputnik 22, Mars 1 and Sputnik 24
short_status: Three launches, 24 October to 4 November 1962: two never left Earth orbit and were never announced. The third, Mars 1, lost its attitude control gas within days and fell silent on 21 March 1963 at 106 million km.
tagline: OKB-1 (USSR) · Soviet Union · Flyby · 1962 · The first attempts Partial
stats: distance at the last contact with Mars 1, a record for its time
radio sessions with Mars 1, and over 3,000 commands sent

facts.label: Launch 1 of 3
facts.value: 2MV-4 No. 3, 24 October 1962, 17:55:04 UTC (20:55 Moscow), Molniya 8K78 vehicle T103-15 from Site 1 at NIIP-5 (Baikonur). Catalogued in the West as Sputnik 22; the USSR announced nothing.

facts.label: Launch 2 of 3
facts.value: 2MV-4 No. 4, 1 November 1962, 16:14:16 UTC (19:14 Moscow), vehicle T103-16 from the same pad. This was the ninth flight of the four-stage 8K78. TASS named it Mars 1 the following day.

facts.label: Launch 3 of 3
facts.value: 2MV-3 No. 1, 4 November 1962, 15:35:15 UTC (18:35 Moscow), vehicle T103-17 from the same pad. Catalogued in the West as Sputnik 24; the USSR announced nothing.

facts.label: Spacecraft type
facts.value: The 2MV second-generation bus, shared between Mars and Venus. A unified sealed orbital module carried guidance, power, thermal control and communications; below it sat either a science module (2MV-2 and 2MV-4, flyby) or a descent capsule (2MV-1 and 2MV-3, impact). Only the flyby versions carried phototelevision cameras.

facts.label: Mars 1 mass and size
facts.value: 893.5 kg, 3.3 m long and 1.1 m in diameter, 4 m across with solar panels and radiators deployed. Solar array area 2.6 square metres, feeding a 42 amp-hour cadmium-nickel battery; interior sealed at 1.1 atmospheres.

facts.label: Mars 1 instruments
facts.value: Phototelevision camera, spectroreflectometer for organic coatings, ozone-band spectrograph, magnetometer on a boom, gas-discharge and scintillation radiation counters, cosmic ray counters, a radio telescope at 150 and 1500 m wavelengths, ion and electron traps, and a micrometeoroid detector.

facts.label: The lander that did not fly
facts.value: 2MV-3 No. 1 carried the only Mars lander of the series: a spheroid roughly 90 cm across with its centre of gravity offset so it would enter blunt face down, instrumented for temperature, pressure, density, atmospheric composition and gamma rays, and buoyant in case it came down in water. Its life-detection instrument had been removed before launch, after it failed to perform adequately in ground tests.

facts.label: Failure, 24 October
facts.value: The Blok L escape stage's S1.5400A1 engine exploded about 17 seconds into the trans-Mars burn when its turbopump failed, traced to leaking lubricant. Twenty-four objects were catalogued, four of them identifiable hardware (the spacecraft, the Blok I, the Blok L and the settling-motor unit) and twenty of them debris; the spacecraft itself reentered on 29 October 1962 and the last object down was the spent Blok L stage on 26 February 1963.

facts.label: Failure, 4 November
facts.value: Cavitation in the core stage propellant lines around T+260 seconds shook the vehicle hard. Chertok recorded a shutdown command reaching the Blok L engine 33 seconds into its burn; other reconstructions say ascent vibration jarred loose an igniter or fuse so the stage never fired. Catalogues disagree about which tracked object was the spacecraft: McDowell's satcat has the spacecraft (00451) decaying on 5 November 1962 and the settling-motor unit (00454) on 19 January 1963, while NSSDCA has a presumed booster decaying on 25 December 1962 and the Mars spacecraft itself on 19 January 1963, and LePage puts the decay of escape-stage and lander components between 27 December 1962 and 19 January 1963.

facts.label: Mars 1's fatal fault
facts.value: A nitrogen valve in the attitude control system never seated properly. By 5 November the entire gas supply had bled out through it. Investigators, including forensic specialists, traced the cause to rosin crumbs from soldering the valve's electromagnet winding lodging under the seat, and reproduced the fault at the factory.

facts.label: How Mars 1 kept working
facts.value: Without three-axis pointing there could be no midcourse correction and no high-gain link, so the craft was put on gyroscopic spin stabilisation to keep the solar panels lit and worked through the low-gain decimetre antenna. Sessions ran at two-day intervals until 13 December 1962, then five-day intervals.

facts.label: Mars 1's operating record
facts.value: 61 radio sessions over about 140 days (37 sessions and over 600 commands in the first month alone), with more than 3,000 commands sent in total. Data returned on cosmic ray intensity, magnetic fields, solar wind ions and meteoroid densities out to 1.24 astronomical units.

facts.label: Last contact with Mars 1
facts.value: 21 March 1963, at 106 million km from Earth (NSSDCA gives 106,760,000 km). This exceeded Mariner 2's final range of about 87 million km on 3 January 1963 and was a record for radio contact with a spacecraft at the time.

facts.label: Mars encounter
facts.value: 19 June 1963, a silent, uncontrolled pass at about 193,000 km according to NSSDCA and Russian sources, or about 197,000 km according to Siddiqi. Mars 1 then continued in solar orbit (perihelion 0.924 AU, aphelion 1.604 AU, eccentricity 0.269, inclination 2.68 degrees, period 519 days).

facts.label: Ground segment
facts.value: The Pluton deep space complex at Yevpatoria in Crimea (NIP-16) handled the sessions. The 2.6 m telescope of the Crimean Astrophysical Observatory also tracked Mars 1, and in February 1963 the same Yevpatoria complex carried out a radar detection of Mars.

facts.label: Names
facts.value: Only Mars 1 was ever named by the USSR. Sputnik 22 and Sputnik 24 are Western catalogue labels; Sputnik 22 was first listed as Sputnik 29 by US Naval Space Command, and Mars 1 appears in some Western lists as Sputnik 23 or Sputnik 30.

timeline: Chertok flies from Vnukovo to the launch range with the main test team. Three rockets and three spacecraft are prepared in parallel on twelve-hour shifts; the window closes on 4 November.
The first Mars rocket is rolled out to Site 1 without ceremony. The same day, in Cuba, the twentieth R-12 missile is being readied for combat duty.

2MV-4 No. 3 launches at 17:55:04 UTC. Three stages work; the Blok L turbopump explodes about 17 seconds into the escape burn and the spacecraft breaks into two dozen pieces. Western catalogues will call the debris Sputnik 22.
The next 8K78, carrying 2MV-4 No. 4, is rolled out to Site 1 for a launch no later than 29 October. It is standing on the pad through the worst hours of the crisis.
Black Saturday. Baikonur goes onto a wartime footing; the Mars rocket is ordered off the pad to make room for a nuclear-armed R-7A. The stand-down comes that evening.

At 14:15 Moscow time the Soviet high-altitude nuclear test K-5 detonates roughly 500 km from the range, blacking out every radio band for over an hour. Mars 1 launches at 16:14:16 UTC once the ionosphere recovers.
Pravda and the radio announcer Yuri Levitan report the launch of a space rocket toward Mars. The craft is named Mars 1.
2MV-3 No. 1, the lander mission, launches at 15:35:15 UTC. The Blok L fails again and the spacecraft stays in Earth orbit, reentering the next day.
Mars 1 has lost all its attitude control nitrogen. Keldysh and Chertok fly to Yevpatoria and conclude there will be no photographs of Mars.
Pravda publishes the trajectory, a photograph of the spacecraft and the science programme. By then the team already knows the craft will not reach Mars alive.
Last contact with Mars 1, at 106 million km, the greatest distance from which any spacecraft had been heard.
Mars 1 makes a silent, uncontrolled pass of Mars at roughly 193,000 km and continues in solar orbit.

images.caption: A NASA three dimensional computer rendering of the Mars 1 spacecraft, a 2MV-4, showing the two solar panels, the umbrella ribbed high gain antenna, the red and white hemispherical thermal radiators, the magnetometer boom and the spherical pennant in its lattice cage on top. The image is a modelled render: the file carries the Blender project name of the NASA intern who built it.

A colour photograph of a 2MV spacecraft standing on its handling ring inside an assembly hall, with a Russian overhead crane load rating sign on the wall behind it. mentallandscape.com labels the frame simply 'Mars-1'; Russian Wikipedia captions it 'Космический аппарат Mars-1 во время тестирования на Земле', Mars 1 during testing on Earth.
images.credit: Soviet factory photograph, photographer unrecorded; via mentallandscape.com and Russian Wikipedia

images.caption: A numbered Soviet line drawing of a 2MV spacecraft in two views, front and side, showing the spherical descent capsule, the umbrella high gain antenna, the solar panels, the thermal radiator hemispheres and the correction engine. The 1962 Mars flyby variant, the 2MV-4 flown as Mars 1, carried an instrument module in place of the descent capsule shown here.
